statement: Baldwin Spencer and Francis James Gillen's The Native Tribes of Central Australia (Macmillan, 1899) and The Arunta: A Study of a Stone Age People (Macmillan, 1927) were, per secondary academic analysis, "overwhelmingly Durkheim's main ethnographic source" for The Elementary Forms of the Religious Life (1912), which used Arrernte/Arunta totemism as its paradigm case of "the simplest and most primitive religion"; Freud's Totem and Taboo (1913) likewise drew directly on Spencer and Gillen's material. These are colonial-era ethnographies produced without informed-consent frameworks; F.J. Gillen's 1896 Engwura festival speeches to the Arrernte are themselves now studied as evidence of the coercive/paternalistic dynamics of the original data-gathering, and the publication of secret-sacred ceremonial/totemic material is a documented, ongoing point of grievance for Arrernte people and later scholars. They should not be presented as neutral or ethically unproblematic authorities.

sources.citation: Spencer, Baldwin, and Francis James Gillen. The Native Tribes of Central Australia. London: Macmillan, 1899.
sources.author: Spencer and Gillen

sources.citation: Durkheim, Émile. Les formes élémentaires de la vie religieuse. 1912; English The Elementary Forms of the Religious Life.
sources.author: Émile Durkheim

does_not_demonstrate: That Spencer and Gillen's material is a neutral, consent-based, or ethically unproblematic ethnographic record
